name: Adino
title: David's Mighty Warrior and Leader of the Three
summary: Adino, known by the nickname "esnitten", held the foremost place among the three mightiest warriors who served King David and acted as their leader. According to the account in 2 Samuel, he swung his weapon against 800 opponents in one battle – a feat that underscores his exceptional warrior skills. He is commonly identified with Jashobeam ben-Hakmoni from 1 Chronicles, where 300 fallen are recorded instead of 800. The discrepancy between these numbers is usually attributed to different manuscript traditions or misreading of numerical letters during copying. Together with Eleazar and Shammah, Adino formed the innermost trio of David's heroes – an elite group that was indispensable for the building and defense of the united kingdom.

keyEvents.title: The Chief of David's Three Mightiest
keyEvents.description: Adino the Eznite was the foremost among David's three mightiest warriors and is regarded as their leader. He rose up against 800 enemies and struck them down in a single encounter, testifying to his exceptional bravery and skill in battle.

keyEvents.title: Parallel Account as Jasobeam
keyEvents.description: In 1 Chronicles he is called Jasobeam son of Hakmoni. There the number of those killed is given as 300, a known textual variation likely due to different manuscript traditions or confusion over numerical letters during the copying process.

keyEvents.title: The Context of David's Elite Warriors
keyEvents.description: The lists of David's heroes provide insight into the military structure surrounding the king. Adino is mentioned in connection with the warriors who strengthened David as leader and helped gather and consolidate the kingdom over all Israel.

keyEvents.title: The Deeds of the Three Mighty Men Against the Philistines
keyEvents.description: Together with Eleazar and Shammah, Adino formed the trio of David's most mighty men. These three performed great heroic feats in battles against the Philistines and other enemies, and their exploits were recorded as examples of extraordinary warrior deeds.

versions.summary: Adino the Eznite was the foremost among David's three mightiest warriors. He is known for having killed 800 men in a single battle and is regarded as one of the bravest and most feared soldiers in King David's army. He is often identified with Jashobeam, who is mentioned in Chronicles.
versions.title: David's Mighty Warrior
versions.reason: [minor] The expression 'esnitten' should be explained more clearly. The Hebrew nickname 'ha-Etsni' is disputed and may be a textual corruption. The connection between Adino and Jasjobam should be formulated with greater nuance.; [minor] Adino was not merely an ordinary warrior, but the leader or head of David's three most powerful men. This role should reflect his leadership position.; [minor] The description states that Adino 'wielded his spear', but the Hebrew text in 2 Sam 23:8 is extremely difficult and disputed. Some manuscripts and translations read the text differently. It is safer to phrase this more neutrally.; [minor] The number 300 versus 800 is a well-known discrepancy between 2 Sam 23:8 and 1 Chr 11:11. This should be mentioned as a textual variation rather than simply presented as fact.; [major] Footnotes are missing. The profile should include footnotes regarding the textual-critical issues surrounding the name Adino/Jasjobam, the numerical difference of 800 versus 300, and the difficult Hebrew text in 2 Sam 23:8.

versions.summary: Adino (also called "esnitten") was the foremost among David's three mightiest warriors and is regarded as their leader and head. According to 2 Samuel, he killed 800 men in a single battle, making him one of the most feared warriors in King David's army. He is often identified with Jashobeam, son of Hachmoni, who is mentioned in 1 Chronicles, where the number of those killed is given as 300. This difference is likely due to textual variations in the ancient manuscripts. Together with Eleazar and Shammah, he formed the inner circle of David's elite warriors.

versions.summary: Adino, by the nickname "esnitten", was the foremost among David's three mightiest warriors and was regarded as their head and leader. In 2 Samuel it is reported that he struck down 800 enemies in a single encounter – an feat that testifies to his exceptional fighting ability and courage. He is usually identified with Jashobeam, son of Hakmoni, who is mentioned in 1 Chronicles, where the number killed is given as 300. This difference is likely due to different manuscript traditions or scribal errors in the transmission of the numbers. Adino belonged to the inner circle of David's elite soldiers together with Eleazar and Shammah, and this trio formed the core of the military leadership that helped establish and defend David's kingdom over Israel.
versions.title: David's Mighty Warrior and Leader of the Three
versions.reason: [major] Hakmoni is strictly speaking the father of Jashobeam (1 Chr 11:11), not directly stated as the father of Adino in 2 Sam 23:8. The identification of Adino with Jashobeam is reasonable, but it should be clarified that this is based on parallel identification. Labeling 'Hakmoni' as a father can be misleading – in 1 Chr 11:11 he is called 'son of Hakmoni' (ben-Hakmoni), which could just as well be a clan name. We retain it with reservation, but this should be noted.; [minor] The summary is well-phrased but resembles version 2 quite closely in structure and wording. It should be rephrased somewhat to distinguish itself more clearly from earlier versions.; [minor] The event 'Part of David's elite warriors' overlaps thematically with events 0 and 3. The description is somewhat general and repeats information from the other events. It could be tightened to provide more distinct information.

footnotes.text: The name 'Adino the Eznite' (Hebrew: עֲדִינוֹ הָעֶצְנִי) in 2 Sam 23:8 is highly debated from a textual-critical perspective. Many scholars believe that the Hebrew text here is corrupt and that the original reading may have been closer to the parallel in 1 Chr 11:11, where the name Jashobeam is used. The Septuagint has a divergent reading that supports this theory.

The difference between 800 killed in 2 Sam 23:8 and 300 killed in 1 Chr 11:11 is one of the most well-known numerical variations in the Old Testament. It is unclear whether this results from a scribal error, different traditions, or references to different events. Numbers in ancient manuscripts were often written with letters that could easily be confused.

David's 'Three Mighty Men' (Hebrew: שְׁלֹשָׁה הַגִּבֹּרִים) formed an inner circle of elite warriors who held a special position in David's military organization. This structure, with an inner circle of outstanding warriors, has parallels in other ancient Near Eastern cultures, including Egyptian and Hittite military systems.

The nickname 'the Eznite' (ha-Etsni) may possibly be derived from a place name or clan name, but its exact meaning is uncertain. Some scholars connect it with the city of Ezni or the clan name Hakmoni used in Chronicles.

Archaeological finds from the Iron Age in Israel and Judah show that professional elite warriors played a crucial role in the kingdom's military structure. Inscriptions and reliefs from contemporary cultures in Egypt and Assyria confirm that small kings often had a small group of selected master warriors in their service.

The designation 'ben-Hakmoni' (בֶּן־חַכְמוֹנִי) in 1 Chr 11:11 can be interpreted either as a patronym ('son of Hakmoni') or as a clan name ('Hakmonite'). This ambiguity is common in Hebrew genealogies and makes it difficult to determine whether Hakmoni was a historical person or a clan/place name.
